ADC Reference Transfer Functions — Vocabulary

72

Eight terms behind the reference-aware ADC conversion. Each has a definition, a project example from the real code, a usage sentence, and a contrast with the term it's most often confused with.

Reference voltage (VR+ / VR−)

89
the conversion's unit of measure
90
91
Definition
92
The voltage pair an ADC compares its input against: VR+ maps to the full-scale code, VR− maps to code 0. Every output code is a fraction of the span between them — the reference literally defines what one "unit" of the result means. Change the reference and the same physical input produces a different code.
93
Project example
94
In silmulator/devices/msp430.py, _adc_reference_voltage() resolves VR+ at conversion time — clock.vcc for AVCC, _veref_v for VEREF, or an ADC_INTERNAL_REF_V lookup for REF_A's outputs. VR− is fixed at AVSS (0 V) in this model. Before commit 58b7e2d, this function didn't exist and VR+ was a hardcoded 3.3.
95
Usage
96
"The RAW code looks huge because you left the 1.2-V reference voltage selected — 1.2 V in, 1.2 V reference, full scale out."
97
Contrast with: supply voltage
98
The supply (AVCC) powers the chip; the reference calibrates the measurement. They coincide only when AVCC is selected as the reference — and then supply drift becomes measurement drift, which is exactly what CPU:VCC 3.0 now lets a SIL test exercise.

Full-scale code (FS)

4095 · 1023 · 255

Definition
108
The maximum code an ADC can output: 2resolution − 1. It is produced when Vin ≥ VR+, so reading it means "at or above the reference" — possibly clipping — never a specific voltage.

Project example
110
msp430_faults.py computes max_code = (1 << resolution) - 1 and clamps with max(0, min(max_code, code)). The audit probe adc_ignores_reference asserts that 1.2 V against the 1.2-V VREF returns exactly 4095 — the input equals the reference, so the result is full scale.

The full-scale code is fixed by ADC:RESOLUTION (ADC12RES); the full-scale voltage is whatever reference is selected. Switching VREF2.5 → AVCC moves the voltage that produces 4095 from 2.5 V to 3.3 V, but 4095 itself never changes.

1. Table 12-1 — One Logical Setting, Two Registers

The single most important idea in this lesson: "this pin has a pull-up" is not one register bit. On the MSP430 (SLAU367P §12.2.4, Table 12-1), the pull resistor is configured by two registers acting together:

  • PxREN — the pull resistor enable: one bit per pin. Set it and a weak resistor is connected to the pin. That is all it says — enabled or not.
  • PxOUT — normally the output register. But when the pin is an input (PxDIR = 0) and PxREN is set, the same bit is repurposed to select which rail the resistor ties to: 0 = pull-down (GND), 1 = pull-up (VCC).

The configuration table (SLAU367P Table 12-1)

PxDIRPxRENPxOUTI/O configuration
00xInput, no pull — floats if nothing drives it
010Input with pull-down
011Input with pull-up
1xdrive levelOutput — PxOUT is back to being the driven value

Two consequences fall straight out of the table:

  1. Pull-up and pull-down are mutually exclusive per pin. There is one resistor and one direction bit — a pin physically cannot pull both ways at once.
  2. Writing PxOUT retargets the pull. Flip the OUT bit of a REN-enabled input pin and the pull-up becomes a pull-down (or vice versa) — no PxREN write involved.
💡 The mental model
PxREN is the switch that connects a resistor to the pin. PxOUT is the rail the far end of that resistor is tied to. One switch, one selectable rail — never two resistors.

Register repurposing is a general MCU pattern

Silicon designers hate wasting register bits. When a pin is an input, its PxOUT bit would otherwise do nothing — so the FR5994 gives it a second job. You have already met this pattern in this codebase:

  • PxOUT — drive level when PxDIR=1; pull direction when PxDIR=0 and PxREN=1 (this lesson).
  • TAxCCRn — a compare value you write, or a capture latch the hardware writes, depending on the CAP bit (lesson 0010's neighbourhood).
  • PxSEL combinations hand the whole pin to a different peripheral entirely.

The modeling rule this forces: the meaning of a stored bit can depend on other stored bits. A simulator that flattens each meaning into its own storage — "a pullup mask" and "a pulldown mask" — has invented registers the part does not have.

2. The Bug — Invented Registers and Inexpressible States

Issue #21 came out of the MSP430 compliance audit. Before commit 4cb71a1, GPIOPort stored the two meanings instead of the two registers:

# silmulator/devices/msp430.py — BEFORE 4cb71a1
@dataclass
class GPIOPort:
    direction: int = 0x00       # 0=input, 1=output (bitmask)
    output:    int = 0x00       # output register value
    input:     int = 0x00       # input register value (injected)
    pullup:    int = 0x00       # pullup enable    ← invented register
    pulldown:  int = 0x00       # pulldown enable  ← invented register

Each SCPI command wrote its own independent mask — _gpio_pullup did p.pullup = int(cmd.params[0], 0) & 0xFF and never looked at pulldown, output, or anything else. Three defects follow, and the audit had a finding for each:

Defect 1 — the inexpressible state (NON_COMPLIANT)

# scripts/audit_msp430.py — the probe BEFORE 4cb71a1 (documents the bug)
def probe_gpio_pull_both(dev):
    """Pull-up and pull-down can be enabled simultaneously on one pin."""
    dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:PULLUP 0x01")
    dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:PULLDOWN 0x01")
    return dev.ports[1].pullup & dev.ports[1].pulldown & 0x01 == 0x01

Both commands succeeded, both masks kept bit 0, and the simulated pin was pulling toward VCC and GND simultaneously — a state with no PxREN/PxOUT encoding. Any SIL test that ran in that configuration validated firmware against physics that does not exist. The audit verdict on PULLUP/PULLDOWN: "Independent PULLUP/PULLDOWN masks allow both pulls on one pin — a state the part cannot express."

Defect 2 — PxOUT changes never retargeted the pull

On hardware, writing PxOUT flips the pull direction of REN-enabled input pins (Table 12-1, consequence 2 above). In the old model the pull direction lived in its own mask, so GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0x00 left a "pullup" in place that real silicon would have just converted to a pull-down.

Defect 3 — input reads ignored pulls entirely (PARTIAL)

# the input-read probe BEFORE 4cb71a1
def probe_gpio_input_ignores_pulls(dev):
    """Input reads ignore enabled pull resistors (no PxREN semantics)."""
    dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:DIRECTION 0x00")
    dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:PULLUP 0xFF")
    return dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:INPUT?") == "0x00"

Enable pull-ups on every pin of an all-input port, read the port — and get 0x00. On the real part every undriven pin reads high through its pull-up. Firmware that relies on a pulled-up button line idling at 1 could never be tested.

⚠ The root cause, in one sentence
The model stored the derived concepts (pull-up set, pull-down set) instead of the documented registers (REN, OUT) — and two copies of one truth can always be driven apart.

3. The Fix — Store the Doc Registers, Derive Everything Else

Commit 4cb71a1 replaces the two invented masks with the one register the documentation defines, and turns the old fields into read-only derived views:

# silmulator/devices/msp430.py — AFTER 4cb71a1
@dataclass
class GPIOPort:
    direction: int = 0x00       # 0=input, 1=output (bitmask)
    output:    int = 0x00       # output register value (PxOUT)
    input:     int = 0x00       # input register value (injected)
    # PxREN (SLAU367P §12.2.4, Table 12-1): one pull resistor enable bit per
    # pin. There is no independent pullup/pulldown register in hardware —
    # while a bit here is set, the matching PxOUT bit selects the pull
    # direction (0=pulldown, 1=pullup).
    resistor_enable: int = 0x00

    @property
    def pullup(self) -> int:
        """Deprecated read-only view: REN-enabled bits with OUT selecting pull-up."""
        return self.resistor_enable & self.output & 0xFF

    @property
    def pulldown(self) -> int:
        """Deprecated read-only view: REN-enabled bits with OUT selecting pull-down."""
        return self.resistor_enable & ~self.output & 0xFF

Worked example — deriving the views

resistor_enable (REN) = 0x0C = 0000 1100   # resistors on pins 3 and 2
output (OUT)          = 0xA5 = 1010 0101   # bit 2 = 1, bit 3 = 0

pullup   = REN & OUT        = 0000 1100 & 1010 0101 = 0000 0100 = 0x04  # pin 2 pulls up
pulldown = REN & ~OUT & 0xFF = 0000 1100 & 0101 1010 = 0000 1000 = 0x08  # pin 3 pulls down

Two invariants now hold by construction, not by discipline:

  • pullup & pulldown == 0 — always. Algebraically, (REN & OUT) & (REN & ~OUT) contains OUT & ~OUT, which is identically zero. The inexpressible state is now unrepresentable.
  • pullup | pulldown == resistor_enable — every enabled resistor pulls exactly one way: (REN & OUT) | (REN & ~OUT) = REN & (OUT | ~OUT) = REN.
📌 Why the & 0xFF?
Python's ~ operates on unbounded ints: ~0xA5 is -166, an infinite string of high bits. The mask clamps the view back to the port's 8 physical lines — the same width discipline lesson 0010 drilled for 16-bit timer registers.

The doc register gets its own SCPI command

Because resistor_enable now exists as real state, the commit registers a first-class command for it — the name the vendor-doc pipeline generates from SLAU367P:

self._register(f"{p}:RESISTOR:ENABLE", lambda cmd, s=pp: self._gpio_ren(cmd, s))

def _gpio_ren(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, p: GPIOPort) -> str:
    """PxREN (SLAU367P §12.2.4, Table 12-1): per-pin pull resistor enable.

    One enable bit per pin; while set, PxOUT's matching bit selects the
    pull direction (0=pulldown, 1=pullup).
    """
    if cmd.is_query:
        return f"0x{p.resistor_enable:02X}"
    if cmd.params:
        p.resistor_enable = int(cmd.params[0], 0) & 0xFF
    return ""

Idiomatic use is now exactly what a datasheet-reader expects: GPIO:PORT1:RESISTOR:ENABLE 0x08 plus GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0x08 = pull-up on pin 3.

4. Deprecated Aliases That Compose the Real Registers

PULLUP and PULLDOWN were not deleted — existing scripts and tests use them. But they no longer own state. A write composes the two real registers; a query returns the derived view:

def _gpio_pullup(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, p: GPIOPort) -> str:
    """Deprecated alias of RESISTOR:ENABLE (SLAU367P §12.2.4, Table 12-1). …"""
    if cmd.is_query:
        return f"0x{p.pullup:02X}"          # derived: REN & OUT
    if cmd.params:
        mask = int(cmd.params[0], 0) & 0xFF
        p.resistor_enable |= mask            # enable the resistor(s)…
        p.output |= mask                     # …and point them at VCC
    return ""

def _gpio_pulldown(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, p: GPIOPort) -> str:
    """Deprecated alias of RESISTOR:ENABLE — see PULLUP. …"""
    if cmd.is_query:
        return f"0x{p.pulldown:02X}"        # derived: REN & ~OUT
    if cmd.params:
        mask = int(cmd.params[0], 0) & 0xFF
        p.resistor_enable |= mask            # enable the resistor(s)…
        p.output &= ~mask                    # …and point them at GND
    return ""

Worked example — the mutual-exclusion trace

StepCommandREN afterOUT afterPULLUP?PULLDOWN?
0(reset)0x000x000x000x00
1PULLUP 0x030x00|0x03 = 0x030x00|0x03 = 0x030x03&0x03 = 0x030x03&~0x03 = 0x00
2PULLDOWN 0x010x03|0x01 = 0x030x03&~0x01 = 0x020x03&0x02 = 0x020x03&~0x02 = 0x01

Pin 0 was pulled up in step 1; step 2's PULLDOWN write flips its OUT bit, so it is now pulled down. Pin 1 keeps its pull-up. The last write per pin wins — exactly what happens on hardware when firmware writes PxOUT — and pullup & pulldown is 0x02 & 0x01 = 0, satisfying the flipped probe: "Pull-up and pull-down are mutually exclusive on one pin (one PxREN bit)."

⚠ Aliases have real side effects now
PULLUP 0x80 sets OUT bit 7. If a later command switches pin 7 to output (PIN:DIRECTION 7,OUTPUT), the pin drives high — because PxOUT is one register with two jobs. That is not a model quirk; it is precisely what the same write sequence does to an FR5994. Conversely, an OUTPUT write now retargets existing pulls, fixing defect 2.

5. Pull-Aware Input Reads — What PxIN Returns

With REN as real state, GPIO:PORTn:INPUT? can finally honour §12.2.4: an undriven input pin with a pull enabled reads the pull level — which is, by repurposing, the PxOUT bit. The read is now a three-way composition:

def _gpio_inp(self, cmd: ScpiCommand, p: GPIOPort) -> str:
    """PxIN (SLAU367P §12.2.1, §12.2.4): combines driven, pulled, and injected bits.

    Output pins read back PxOUT. Undriven input pins read the pull level
    (PxOUT's bit) when PxREN enables a resistor on that pin; input pins
    with no pull enabled read the externally injected value, as today.
    """
    driven        = p.output & p.direction
    undriven_mask = ~p.direction & 0xFF
    pulled        = p.output & p.resistor_enable & undriven_mask
    injected      = p.input & undriven_mask & ~p.resistor_enable
    effective     = driven | pulled | injected
    return f"0x{effective & 0xFF:02X}"

Worked example — all three sources at once

direction (DIR)       = 0xF0 = 1111 0000   # pins 7-4 output, pins 3-0 input
output (OUT)          = 0xA5 = 1010 0101
resistor_enable (REN) = 0x0C = 0000 1100   # pulls on pins 3, 2
input (injected)      = 0x03 = 0000 0011   # external world drives pins 1, 0 high

driven   = OUT & DIR                 = 0xA5 & 0xF0          = 0xA0   # pins 7-4 read their drive
undriven = ~DIR & 0xFF               =                        0x0F
pulled   = OUT & REN & undriven      = 0xA5 & 0x0C & 0x0F   = 0x04   # pin 2: pull-up → 1; pin 3: pull-down → 0
injected = IN & undriven & ~REN      = 0x03 & 0x0F & ~0x0C  = 0x03   # pins 1, 0: no pull → injected value

effective = 0xA0 | 0x04 | 0x03 = 0xA7       # GPIO:PORT1:INPUT? → "0xA7"

Pin by pin: 7–4 return OUT's high nibble (1010); pin 3 has REN set and OUT bit 3 = 0 → pull-down → reads 0; pin 2 has REN set and OUT bit 2 = 1 → pull-up → reads 1; pins 1–0 have no resistor → the injected 11 passes through.

The flipped audit probe

# scripts/audit_msp430.py — AFTER 4cb71a1
def probe_gpio_input_ignores_pulls(dev):
    """Undriven input pins with REN enabled read PxOUT's pull level (§12.2.4)."""
    dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:DIRECTION 0x00")
    dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:RESISTOR:ENABLE 0xFF")
    dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0xFF")
    return dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:INPUT?") == "0xFF"

All-input port, all resistors enabled, all pointing at VCC → every pin reads high. GPIO:PORTn:INPUT moved PARTIAL → COMPLIANT, and test_input_reflects_enabled_pullup dropped its xfail marker.

⚠ A deliberate model limitation
Look at the injected line: & ~p.resistor_enable masks the injected value out on every REN-enabled pin. The model treats a REN pin as undriven — the pull always wins. Real hardware has drive strength: an external driver overpowers a ~35 kΩ pull. Silmulator has no drive-strength model, so to simulate "external device drives a pulled-up line low" you must clear that pin's REN bit for the duration (see Scenario C). Know this before writing button tests.

6. Pin-Index Validation — 8 Lines Means 0–7 (-222)

The same commit closes a neighbouring hole. Ports have exactly 8 I/O lines, but the per-pin commands accepted any integer and shifted with it:

# BEFORE: GPIO:PORT1:PIN:VALUE 12,1  →  p.output |= (1 << 12)  =  0x1000
#         an "8-bit" register now holds 0x1000 — every later mask read is corrupt

The fix is a shared validator, called by both _gpio_pin_dir and _gpio_pin_val before any shift happens:

@staticmethod
def _validate_pin(pin: int) -> None:
    """Reject pin indexes outside an 8-bit port's 8 I/O lines (SLAU367P §12.2)."""
    if not 0 <= pin <= 7:
        raise ScpiError(-222, f"Pin index out of range (0-7): {pin}")

_gpio_pin_dir also gained a rejection for made-up modes — previously PIN:DIRECTION 0,BANANA fell through every branch and was silently ignored:

val = cmd.params[1].upper()
if val in ("OUTPUT", "1", "OUT"):
    p.direction |= (1 << pin)
elif val in ("INPUT", "0", "IN"):
    p.direction &= ~(1 << pin)
else:
    raise ScpiError(-224, f"Illegal pin mode: {val}")

GPIO:PORT1:PIN:VALUE 12,1-222 "Data out of range"The parameter is the right type (an integer) but outside the representable range 0–7 — the same code lesson 0010 used for over-width register writes.
GPIO:PORT1:PIN:DIRECTION 0,BANANA-224 "Illegal parameter value"A token outside the permitted value set — a pin is input or output, no third mode exists (§12.2.3). Same code as ADC:REFERENCE BANANA.

# AFTER 4cb71a1
def probe_gpio_pin_index_unvalidated(dev):
    """Pin numbers beyond 7 are rejected with -222 on an 8-bit port."""
    dev.process("GPIO:PORT1:PIN:VALUE 12,1")
    return _errors(dev) == 1 and dev.ports[1].output == 0

7. Why This Matters for SIL Testing — and What the Audit Says Now

The bug class that was invisible

Consider firmware that configures a pulled-up button line the way TI's own examples do:

/* firmware under test — button on P1.3, active low */
P1DIR &= ~BIT3;      /* input                       */
P1REN |=  BIT3;      /* enable the pull resistor    */
P1OUT |=  BIT3;      /* …and make it a pull-UP      */
while (P1IN & BIT3) { }   /* wait for press (line falls) */
  • Old model: the P1OUT write did nothing to the pull, and INPUT? ignored pulls anyway — the idle line read 0, so the "wait for press" loop exited instantly. A SIL test could not tell working button code from broken button code. Worse, firmware that set both pulls (a real bug — random idle level, wasted current) tested fine.
  • New model: the same sequence gives resistor_enable bit 3 and output bit 3, and INPUT? returns bit 3 = 1 while unpressed. The idle level is right, and the both-pulls state cannot even be represented to test against.

Commit 4cb71a1 removed @pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True) from four tests in tests/test_msp430_edge_cases.py — the ledger-of-known-bugs pattern from earlier lessons paying off again:

The generated spec (custom_blocks/msp430fr5994_generated.json) had carried GPIO:PORT1:RESISTOR:ENABLE as a CONFLICT — the doc-derived command existed in the model only as the structurally different PULLUP/PULLDOWN pair, with an equivalence_note spelling out the inexpressible-state problem. Now the model implements the doc command directly:

  • The JSON entry's model_equivalent/equivalence_note escape hatch was deleted, replaced by an ordinary valid_values + echo_check probe.
  • Diff counts moved CONFLICT 1 → 0, MATCH 17 → 18; PULLUP/PULLDOWN reappear as MISSING_FROM_GENERATED — the correct bucket for simulator conveniences with no doc basis.
  • test_flags_structural_pull_resistor_conflict was renamed test_pull_resistor_conflict_resolved and now asserts the command is a MATCH; test_conflicts_are_warnings_not_blockers asserts counts()[CONFLICT] == 0.

The report header moved from 26.7% (27 of 101 families) to 34.3% (35 of 102 families): RESISTOR:ENABLE is a new COMPLIANT family, and PULLUP, PULLDOWN, INPUT/IN, PIN:VALUE/PIN, and PIN:DIRECTION all flipped to COMPLIANT.

💡 The design rule
Model the registers the documentation names, and derive every human-friendly concept from them. Stored state answers "what did the doc say exists?"; properties answer "what does that state mean?". If two stored fields can contradict each other, one of them is a bug waiting for a probe.

8. Often Confused

ConfusionThe distinction
"PxREN = 1 means pull-up" PxREN only connects the resistor. Direction is the PxOUT bit: 0 = pull-down, 1 = pull-up. RESISTOR:ENABLE 0xFF with OUTPUT 0x00 is eight pull-downs.
"PULLUP? returns what I last wrote to PULLUP" The query returns the derived view REN & OUT right now. A later PULLDOWN or OUTPUT write changes it without any PULLUP command being sent. Aliases are windows onto REN/OUT, not stores.
"PULLUP then PULLDOWN on the same pin → both active" The second write clears the pin's OUT bit while REN stays set — the pull flips down. Last write per pin wins; pullup & pulldown is identically 0.
"The OUT bit of an input pin does nothing" With REN set it selects the pull direction; and it is still latched, so flipping the pin to output later drives that level. Repurposing means the bit always matters.
-222 vs -224 on the GPIO commands -222 "Data out of range": numeric but outside 0–7 (PIN:VALUE 12,1). -224 "Illegal parameter value": token outside the permitted set (PIN:DIRECTION 0,BANANA).

"port.pullup = 0x01 still works in tests" pullup/pulldown are @property without setters — assignment raises AttributeError. Test fixtures must write resistor_enable and output, the same registers firmware would.

Q1. Fresh device. A script sends GPIO:PORT1:PULLUP 0x01 then GPIO:PORT1:PULLDOWN 0x01. What does GPIO:PORT1:PULLUP? now return?

  • 0x00 — the PULLDOWN write flipped the pin's OUT bit, so the derived pull-up view is empty
  • 0x01 — the pullup mask was set and PULLDOWN doesn't touch it
  • SCPI error -224 — conflicting pull configuration
  • 0x01 — because the resistor is still enabled

Q2. With resistor_enable = 0x0C and output = 0xA5, what do the derived views return?

  • pullup = 0x04, pulldown = 0x08
  • pullup = 0x0C, pulldown = 0x00
  • pullup = 0x08, pulldown = 0x04
  • pullup = 0x0C, pulldown = 0x0C

Q3. Port 1 is configured: DIRECTION 0x00, RESISTOR:ENABLE 0x0F, OUTPUT 0xF3, and the test injects input = 0x30. What does GPIO:PORT1:INPUT? return?

  • 0x33
  • 0x30
  • 0x03
  • 0xF3

Q4. Why are pullup and pulldown implemented as @property on GPIOPort instead of stored fields kept in sync by the handlers?

  • So the views can never disagree with REN/OUT — the impossible state becomes unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged
  • Properties are faster than dataclass fields
  • Dataclasses cannot mix stored fields with anything else
  • Purely to keep old SCPI scripts working

Q5. A script sends GPIO:PORT1:PULLUP 0x80, and much later GPIO:PORT1:PIN:DIRECTION 7,OUTPUT. What is pin 7 doing now, and why?

  • Driving high — the PULLUP write set OUT bit 7, which becomes the drive level once the pin is an output
  • Still pulling up weakly — REN overrides direction
  • Driving low — OUT is cleared when a pin changes direction
  • SCPI error -222 — direction changes are rejected while REN is set

10. Scenarios — Check Your Understanding

Scenario A: A teammate configures "pull-ups on the whole port" with GPIO:PORT1:DIRECTION 0x00 + GPIO:PORT1:RESISTOR:ENABLE 0xFF, then reads INPUT? and gets 0x00. "The pull-ups are broken!" What actually happened, and what one command fixes it?
Show answer

They never selected a direction. After *RST, output = 0x00, and on input pins with REN set the OUT bit is the direction select: 0 = pull-down. So they configured eight perfectly working pull-downs, and every undriven pin correctly reads 0 — pulled = OUT & REN & undriven = 0x00 & 0xFF & 0xFF = 0x00.

The fix: GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0xFF. Now pulled = 0xFF & 0xFF & 0xFF = 0xFF and INPUT? returns 0xFF — this exact triple is the flipped audit probe. The lesson in one line: REN answers "resistor?", OUT answers "which rail?" — you must answer both questions.

Scenario B: A legacy test does PULLUP 0xFF then PULLDOWN 0xFF and asserts both queries return 0xFF (it was written against the old model, where they did). Predict its result today, trace the register state, and say what the test should assert.
Show answer 
PULLUP  0xFF   →  REN |= 0xFF → 0xFF ;  OUT |= 0xFF  → 0xFF
PULLDOWN 0xFF  →  REN |= 0xFF → 0xFF ;  OUT &= ~0xFF → 0x00
PULLUP?    →  REN & OUT        =  0xFF & 0x00  →  "0x00"   ← assertion fails here
PULLDOWN?  →  REN & ~OUT & 0xFF = 0xFF & 0xFF  →  "0xFF"

The test fails on the PULLUP? assertion — and that failure is the fix working. The old assertion demanded an inexpressible state (both pulls on every pin). The corrected test asserts mutual exclusion, like test_pullup_pulldown_mutually_exclusive: not (ports[1].pullup & ports[1].pulldown), plus last-write-wins: after the sequence above, all eight pins pull down. If the test's real intent was "resistors enabled everywhere," it should assert RESISTOR:ENABLE? == 0xFF — that is the register that actually carries that meaning.

Scenario C: You are writing a SIL test for the active-low button firmware from section 7 (P1.3 input, REN set, OUT set). Write the SCPI to model the idle state, then simulate the button press. Why doesn't GPIO:PORT1:INPUT 0x00 (injecting a low) work on its own, and what is the workaround?
Show answer 
GPIO:PORT1:PIN:DIRECTION 3,INPUT   ← P1.3 is an input
GPIO:PORT1:RESISTOR:ENABLE 0x08    ← REN bit 3: resistor connected
GPIO:PORT1:OUTPUT 0x08             ← OUT bit 3: pull-UP
GPIO:PORT1:INPUT?                  → bit 3 reads 1 (idle, unpressed)  ✓

# simulate the press — injection alone is NOT enough:
GPIO:PORT1:INPUT 0x00              ← masked out! injected = IN & undriven & ~REN
GPIO:PORT1:INPUT?                  → bit 3 STILL reads 1 (the pull wins)

# workaround: a pressed button is a strong external driver — model it by
# disconnecting the resistor for the duration of the press:
GPIO:PORT1:RESISTOR:ENABLE 0x00    ← REN off: pin is now injection-driven
GPIO:PORT1:INPUT 0x00
GPIO:PORT1:INPUT?                  → bit 3 reads 0 — press observed

The injected value on a REN-enabled pin is masked by & ~p.resistor_enable in _gpio_inp — the model has no drive-strength arbitration, so the pull always wins where REN is set. Real hardware would let the button (a hard short to GND) overpower the ~35 kΩ pull-up without touching P1REN. The REN-toggle workaround keeps the test honest; restore RESISTOR:ENABLE 0x08 on release. If your firmware polls REN itself, document this divergence in the test.

ANDing with 0xFF clamps the result to the port's 8 physical I/O lines — the same explicit-width discipline lesson 0010 required for 16-bit timer registers. In C, a uint8_t variable is physically 8 bits, so ~out is already truncated by the type; Python has no such type, so the model must enforce width by hand.` }, {id:'d3',ch:'derive',type:'mc', q:'For ANY values of resistor_enable and output, what is pullup & pulldown?', opts:[ {t:'0 — identically: (REN & OUT) & (REN & ~OUT) contains OUT & ~OUT, which is always zero',c:true, w:'Correct. Every enabled resistor pulls exactly one way, so the two views partition REN. Issue #21's example: with independent pullup/pulldown masks, "GPIO:PORT1:PULLUP 0x01" then "GPIO:PORT1:PULLDOWN 0x01" left both masks with bit 0 set — one pin pulling toward VCC and GND at once. Queries return the derived properties: PULLUP? → f"0x{p.pullup:02X}" (REN & OUT), PULLDOWN? → f"0x{p.pulldown:02X}" (REN & ~OUT & 0xFF). "Compose the real registers" means the aliases own no storage: every observable effect is a combination of writes to resistor_enable and output — the two registers SLAU367P documents. Old scripts keep working (backward compatibility is the only reason the commands survive, marked Deprecated in their docstrings), but they can no longer construct a state the registers can't hold: PULLDOWN after PULLUP retargets pins instead of contradicting them.` }, {id:'a3',ch:'alias',type:'mc', q:'Why did commit 4cb71a1 keep PULLUP/PULLDOWN at all instead of deleting them along with the stored masks?', opts:[ {t:'Backward compatibility — existing SCPI scripts and tests use them; re-expressed as compositions of REN/OUT they stay correct while impossible states stay impossible',c:true, w:'Correct. The deprecation pattern: keep the old surface, reroute it through the new single source of truth, document the preferred replacement (RESISTOR:ENABLE + OUTPUT).'}, {t:'SLAU367P documents PULLUP and PULLDOWN commands',c:false,w:'It documents registers (PxREN/PxOUT), not SCPI commands. The vendor-doc diff actually classifies PULLUP/PULLDOWN as MISSING_FROM_GENERATED — simulator conveniences with no doc basis.'}, {t:'The GUI depends on them and cannot be updated',c:false,w:'Nothing in the commit says that; the motivation in the docstrings is the alias/deprecation relationship to RESISTOR:ENABLE.'}, {t:'They are faster than separate REN and OUTPUT writes',c:false,w:'Convenience, not performance — one command instead of two is ergonomics; the reason they SURVIVE is compatibility.'}, ] }, {id:'a4',ch:'alias',type:'mc', q:'A script sends GPIO:PORT1:PULLUP 0x80 and later switches pin 7 to output. The identical write sequence on a real FR5994 also drives high.'}, {t:'The alias set DIR bit 7, making the pin an output immediately',c:false,w:'Neither alias touches direction — only resistor_enable and output.'}, {t:'The resistor keeps pulling while the pin drives, causing a simulated short',c:false,w:'The model\'s input read puts driven pins entirely under OUT & DIR; there is no contention model. Before: return dev.ports[1].pullup & dev.ports[1].pulldown & 0x01 == 0x01 — docstring "Pull-up and pull-down can be enabled simultaneously on one pin." After: return dev.ports[1].pullup & dev.ports[1].pulldown & 0x01 == 0 — docstring "Pull-up and pull-down are mutually exclusive on one pin (one PxREN bit)." Output pins (DIR=1): read back PxOUT — "driven". 2. Input pins with a pull (DIR=0, REN=1): read PxOUT's bit too, but with a different meaning — it is the pull level (0=pulled low, 1=pulled high). PxREN

SLAU367P §12.2.4, Table 12-1 — pull resistor enable register
Definition
The MSP430's per-port pull-resistor-enable register: one bit per pin. While a bit is set on an input pin, a weak resistor is connected to that pin — and the pin's PxOUT bit selects the direction (0 = pull-down, 1 = pull-up). PxREN itself never encodes a direction; it is one enable bit whose direction lives in another register.
Project example
Commit 4cb71a1 added resistor_enable: int = 0x00 to GPIOPort in silmulator/devices/msp430.py and registered GPIO:PORTn:RESISTOR:ENABLE (_gpio_ren) to read/write it as an 8-bit mask — replacing the invented independent pullup/pulldown fields the audit had flagged NON_COMPLIANT.
Usage
"REN bit 3 is set but you never wrote PxOUT — so that's a pull-down on the button line, which is why it idles low."
Contrast with: PxOUT
PxREN answers "is a resistor connected?"; PxOUT answers "to which rail?" (and, on output pins, "what level do I drive?"). Neither register alone defines a pull-up — the setting only exists as the conjunction of the two, which is exactly what the old two-mask model got wrong.

Register repurposing

one latch, two jobs
Definition
A hardware-design economy where one register bit means different things depending on other configuration state, instead of silicon spending a dedicated register per concept. The modeling consequence: the meaning of stored state is contextual, so a simulator must store the documented registers and derive meanings — not flatten each meaning into its own storage.
Project example
PxOUT is the drive level when PxDIR=1 but the pull-direction select when PxDIR=0 and PxREN=1 (SLAU367P Table 12-1). The GPIOPort comment added in 4cb71a1 spells it out: "There is no independent pullup/pulldown register in hardware — while a bit here is set, the matching PxOUT bit selects the pull direction." Same pattern as TAxCCRn's compare-vs-capture dual role behind the CAP bit.
Usage
"Careful — that register is repurposed: writing P1OUT to pick pull directions will also be the drive level if anyone flips P1DIR later."
Contrast with: register aliasing
Aliasing (lesson 0010: PERIOD IS TAxCCR0) is two names for one register with one meaning. Repurposing is one register whose single stored value carries different meanings in different modes. Aliasing is fixed by delegating storage; repurposing is fixed by deriving meaning at read time.

Inexpressible state

a configuration no silicon can reach
Definition
A simulator state that no sequence of register writes can produce on the real part — it lies outside the hardware's reachable state space. A model that can hold one lets SIL tests run against physics that will never occur, so any pass observed there transfers nothing to hardware.
Project example
Before 4cb71a1, GPIO:PORT1:PULLUP 0x01 followed by GPIO:PORT1:PULLDOWN 0x01 left both independent masks with bit 0 set — one pin pulling toward VCC and GND simultaneously. probe_gpio_pull_both reproduced it on demand; the fix makes it unrepresentable, since pullup & pulldown is (REN & OUT) & (REN & ~OUT) = 0 identically.
Usage
"Don't add a boolean for that — you'd create an inexpressible state the moment it disagrees with the register it summarises."
Contrast with: invalid input
An invalid input (PIN:VALUE 12,1, ADC:REFERENCE BANANA) is caught at the boundary with a SCPI error. An inexpressible state is worse: every individual write looked legal, but their combination landed the stored model somewhere hardware cannot go. Validation stops the former; only correct state structure prevents the latter.

Derived view

computed at read time, never stored
Definition
A value computed on demand from stored state rather than kept as its own field. Because a derived view has no storage, it can never disagree with its sources — invariants hold by construction instead of by every writer's discipline.
Project example
4cb71a1 turned GPIOPort.pullup and .pulldown into read-only @propertys: resistor_enable & output & 0xFF and resistor_enable & ~output & 0xFF. With REN=0x0C, OUT=0xA5 they yield 0x04/0x08 — always disjoint, always uniting to REN. The & 0xFF clamps Python's unbounded ~ to the port's 8 lines.
Usage
"Make it a derived view — if we store a second copy, some code path will eventually update one and not the other."
Contrast with: cached/synced copy
A synced copy is stored and updated by every writer that remembers to; it is fast to read but can drift (the pre-fix pull masks were effectively unsynced copies). A derived view trades a trivial recompute for structural correctness. Cache only when profiling says you must.

Deprecated alias

old surface, new plumbing
Definition
A command kept for backward compatibility after its underlying model changed. It owns no state of its own: writes are re-expressed as compositions of the real registers, and queries return derived views — so old scripts keep working, but the alias can no longer construct states the new model forbids.
Project example
GPIO:PORTn:PULLUP <mask> now performs resistor_enable |= mask; output |= mask, and PULLDOWN <mask> performs resistor_enable |= mask; output &= ~mask; both queries return the derived properties. Their docstrings open with "Deprecated alias of RESISTOR:ENABLE", and the vendor-doc diff files them under MISSING_FROM_GENERATED — simulator conveniences with no doc basis.
Usage
"Keep PULLUP as a deprecated alias for the old test suites, but route it through REN and OUT so it can't lie about what the hardware can do."
Contrast with: removal
Deleting the commands would break every existing script for zero semantic gain; keeping them as independent stores would preserve the bug. The alias is the middle path: compatibility of surface, correctness of state. The cost: aliases now have honest side effects (PULLUP sets OUT bits that later become drive levels).

Pull-up / pull-down

a weak resistor to VCC or GND
Definition
A weak resistor (tens of kΩ) tying an otherwise-undriven input pin to a rail so it reads a defined level instead of floating: pull-up to VCC (reads 1), pull-down to GND (reads 0). Any real driver on the line overpowers it. On the MSP430 the two are mutually exclusive per pin: one PxREN enable, one PxOUT direction bit.
Project example
The flipped audit probe: DIRECTION 0x00 + RESISTOR:ENABLE 0xFF + OUTPUT 0xFF makes GPIO:PORT1:INPUT? return 0xFF — eight undriven inputs all reading high through pull-ups. Swap OUTPUT 0x00 and the same resistors become pull-downs and the port reads 0x00.
Usage
"The button shorts the line to ground, so configure a pull-up — active-low, idles at 1, pressed reads 0."
Contrast with: driven level
A driven level (an output driver, or a pressed button) is strong: it sets the line regardless of pulls. A pull only decides the level when nothing drives the line. Silmulator models no drive-strength contest — on a REN-enabled pin the pull always wins and injected values are masked out, so simulating an external override means clearing REN first.

Undriven pin

nobody is asserting a level
Definition
An input pin with no active driver — the MCU isn't driving it (PxDIR = 0) and no external device is asserting a level. In hardware an undriven pin with no pull floats: it reads unpredictably and wastes power in the input buffer. With a pull enabled it reads the pull level deterministically.
Project example
_gpio_inp partitions each port: driven = output & direction, then within undriven_mask = ~direction & 0xFF, REN-enabled pins read output & resistor_enable (the pull level) and the rest read the injected value. An undriven input pin with REN set therefore reads the OUT bit — the pull-aware read issue #21 added.
Usage
"That input reads 0x00 only because every pin is undriven with a pull-down — inject a value or flip OUT before concluding the port is dead."
Contrast with: floating pin
Floating is what an undriven, un-pulled pin does in the physical world — an indeterminate level the simulator can't honestly represent (it models the injected value, default 0, instead). An undriven pin with a pull is not floating: its level is defined. "Undriven" describes who is driving (nobody); "floating" describes the resulting indeterminacy when there's also no pull.

Single source of truth (registers)

store the doc registers; derive the concepts
Definition
The modeling discipline of storing exactly the registers the documentation defines — once each — and computing every other representation from them. One write updates every view; no two copies of a fact exist to disagree; states outside the registers' reachable combinations cannot be represented at all.
Project example
GPIOPort stores direction, output, input, resistor_enable — the SLAU367P register set — and derives pullup/pulldown as properties. Every command, old or new, ultimately reads or writes those stored registers: RESISTOR:ENABLE directly, the deprecated aliases by composition, INPUT? by combining three of them.
Usage
"Before adding a field to the device model, ask which SLAU367P register it corresponds to — if the answer is 'none', it's probably a view that should be derived from a single source of truth."
Contrast with: one store per concept
Storing each user-facing concept (a pull-up mask, a pull-down mask, a period value) feels convenient but multiplies the places one hardware fact lives — the root cause behind both this fix and lesson 0010's PERIOD/TAxCCR0 double-store. Concepts are cheap to derive; contradictions are expensive to debug.
